To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

both self and emotion attributions to others activate the MPFC and that self judgments selectively activate medial PFC subregions, whereas other judgments selectively activate lateral PFC and medial occipital regions.

(1) self and other judgments about emotion activate a network of common regions including the MPFC, superior temporal gyrus (STG), and posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), and (2) self judgments selectively recruit the MPFC and left temporal cortex, while other judgments selectively recruit the left lateral pre-frontal cortex (LPFC) and medial occipital regions.

self and other judgments of emotion activate overlapping and distinct neural systems, with common regions including the medial prefront and superior temporal gyrus and distinct regions including the left temporal cortex (self) and the medial and lateral prefrontal cortices (other).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cognitive and neural processes involved in attributing emotional states to self or other individuals.
the neural substrates of mental state attribution, with an emphasis on the attribution of emotional states.
the neural basis of social cognitive processes, and the role of these processes in social behavior.

the MPFC and temporal lobe regions are involved in both self and other evaluations of emotion, whereas lateral PFC and occipital regions are selectively involved in self and other evaluations, respectively
the neural substrates of self and other emotion attributions involve common and distinct regions of frontal and parietal cortex.

the MPFC is a critical region involved in the evaluation of both the self and other, but that the lateral PFC and medial occipital regions are selectively recruited for the evaluation of other emotional states.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the medial PFC, superior temporal gyrus and posterior cingulate are all activated by both self and other emotion judgments.
we have shown that the medial prefrontial cortex is involved in both self and other evaluations of emotion and that the lateral prefrontal regions are selectively involved in self evaluations.
the neural systems supporting the attribution of emotional states to self and others share common regions of activation in the MPFC, the posterior cingulat/precuneus and the temporal lobe.
The main takeaway from our work is that
self and other judgments of emotion recruit common and distinct neural systems, and that these systems are likely involved in the attribution of mental states more broadly.
there are commonalities and differences in the neural substrates underlying self and other judgments of emotional states.

the neural systems supporting the attribution of emotion to self and other are partially shared, and that these systems may be organized in a way that reflects the internal versus external nature of the information that is being processed.
